So from what I understand is that for the most part these problems are of the past, and that with the advent of yum there are no significant (dis)advantages to other packet managers?

I think that would be a gross over-simplication of things. You kinda have to understand the structure of an RPM to understand the issue of dependency hell. Basically, in the RPM you can specify which other RPM's are required. This unto itself isn't a problem. The problem comes when you pull in RPM packages that are out of your distro and they use other dependencies that you have technically met, but they call them by different names. Thus causing you to do weird shit like rpm -ivh package.rpm --nodeps and shit like that. The more of that you do, the weirder your system gets and the less stable things are.
How do other packet managers prevent this then?

I think, on the whole, they all suffer from a similar plight, the difference between debian and other distros with package management being that most of the other distros still use some portion of debian as the base for their distro, so there isn't as huge a delta between the parent and child. This would not be true as with Ubuntu, which has now fled far afield from Debian. Other package systems, like portage have similar challenges but get around this by including just about anything into the ports tree, thus allowing folks to include dependencies, and so forth.

One solution, floated by Canonical, was to make binary packages inclusive of all their dependencies. Essentially, taking the OS X approach. That is another debate altogether, but WOULD solve (almost completely) the whole dependency game.

Once upon a day it took me two days to search, download and install all dependencies for some application, which I don't remember the name of. After installing Debian for first time, I never went back to distros with rpms.
Now? Yes. Back then, yum wasn't around. I got used to aptitude and never cared about yum.

yum == yellowdog update manager. History lesson! Yellowdog was a distro specifically for PPC, and they tried to address the RPM dependency fiasco. It works, and works well, provided that all RPM's have a consistent naming convention for dependencies and that those dependencies have compiled feature parity, then it works as well as Debian's apt-get, etc.

The reason Debian does better in this regard is because for a long time there were no debian off-shoots.

I'm a huge Debian fan and prefer .deb distributions (making Ubuntu tolerable), but I don't hate RPM distributions. Yum is a nice tool, though still not as mature as apt-get. My biggest complaint about Yum would be that it's too chatty with the server. I like apt-get's explicit step to download all the latest information, then work offline until it needs to fetch packages. That part is analgous to Subversion vs. Git.

I got my start on Linux with Red Hat and Fedora Core and got to witness Yum entering the scene. It was a godsend that changed the way I used Linux. Since then the difference between the major distributions has shrunk.

I don't like CentOS and Red Hat as desktop systems -- it's been years since I've used Fedora -- because of its meager package selection. Just getting a proper media player installed is a lot of work. In contrast, Debian's repositories have everything I need and I don't need to putz around piecing a working system together. It's just more mature all around. But none of that has anything to do with the specific formats of .deb and .rpm.

I've faced far fewer "dependency hell" problems with .deb based distros. RHEL with corporate support has been ok so far, and RedHat has been responsive with fixes. All other RPM based distros drive me up the wall with dependency hell, specially the newer Fedora releases after 2010-11.

My personal experience has been unsolvable RPM dependency hell. However that was honestly back in 2003 and 2004. I've tried the gamut of package management systems but I fully admit to avoiding anything RPM since then.
